details:
**The Death of Marat**
David's 1793 painting of the murdered radical journalist Jean-Paul Marat, editor of The Friend of the People. Marat slumps in his bathtub (he bathed to soothe a chronic skin disease) wearing a turban-like head cloth, holding a quill in his drooping right arm and a letter in his left hand. A bloody knife lies on the floor, and a wooden crate serves as his desk. It is often called a secular "Pietà of the Revolution."

**Charlotte Corday**
The Girondin sympathizer who stabbed Marat in his bath in 1793. In David's painting, Marat holds her letter, which reads "My great unhappiness gives me a right to your kindness," the excuse she used to get in to see him.

**The Oath of the Horatii**
David's 1784 Neoclassical masterpiece, based on a legend told by Livy. Three Roman brothers, the Horatii, stretch out their arms in a salute and swear to fight to the death for Rome as their father holds up three swords. On the right, their mother, sisters, and children weep, since one sister is engaged to one of the enemy Curiatii. The scene is framed by three arches on columns.

**The Death of Socrates**
A 1787 painting of the Athenian philosopher about to drink hemlock in prison. Socrates points upward with one hand as he reaches for the cup with the other. The grieving disciple handing him the cup covers his eyes, Crito grips Socrates's leg, Plato sits dejected at the foot of the bed, and in the background men climb a staircase.

**The Lictors Bring to Brutus the Bodies of His Sons**
A 1789 painting of Lucius Junius Brutus, founder of the Roman Republic, who ordered the execution of his sons for plotting to restore the monarchy. Brutus broods in shadow beneath a statue of Roma (inscribed "DEA ROMA") while lictors carry in the bodies on the left. On the right, his anguished wife, in orange, clutches their daughters, one of whom faints, and a servant covers her face with a shawl.

**The Intervention of the Sabine Women**
A painting David began while imprisoned after the fall of Robespierre. Hersilia, in white with outstretched arms, throws herself between her husband Romulus and her father Titus Tatius to stop the battle between the Romans and Sabines, as other women hold up their babies. David described his aim as a return to "pure Greek" style.

**Napoleon Crossing the Alps**
David's heroic equestrian portrait of Napoleon in a billowing red-orange cloak on a rearing horse, pointing upward as he leads his army through the Great St. Bernard Pass. Rocks in the foreground are carved with the names Bonaparte, Hannibal, and Karolus Magnus (Charlemagne), and soldiers drag cannons in the background. David also painted Napoleon in His Study at the Tuileries.

**The Coronation of Napoleon**
David's huge painting of Napoleon's 1804 coronation at Notre-Dame Cathedral. Instead of showing Napoleon crowning himself, as originally planned, it shows him crowning the kneeling Joséphine as Pope Pius VII looks on.

**Portrait of Madame Récamier**
A portrait of the Parisian socialite Juliette Récamier in a simple white Empire-waist dress and black headband, reclining on an antique-style sofa and glancing over her shoulder.

**Mars Being Disarmed by Venus and the Three Graces**
David's last major painting, made in exile in Brussels. Venus offers Mars a crown of flowers, a Cupid unties his sandal, and the Graces take his weapons and offer him wine.

**Jacobin politics and The Tennis Court Oath**
David was a Jacobin and an ally of Robespierre, served in the National Convention (including a brief term as its president), and voted for the execution of Louis XVI. His unfinished Tennis Court Oath depicts the 1789 pledge of the Third Estate deputies. After Robespierre's fall he was imprisoned, and he later became Napoleon's official painter.

**Portrait of Antoine Lavoisier and His Wife**
David's 1788 double portrait of the chemist Antoine Lavoisier seated at a table of scientific instruments with his wife Marie-Anne, who leans on his shoulder. Marie-Anne had studied painting with David.

**Leonidas at Thermopylae**
A late painting of the Spartan king Leonidas before his last stand against the Persians. On the left, a soldier carves a farewell message into the rock of the mountain pass.

**Belisarius Begging for Alms**
An early David painting of the blind Byzantine general Belisarius, fallen from favor and reduced to begging, being recognized by a soldier who once served under him.
